title: Your own petition
hookLine: putting a short personal request into your own words, the way Sikhs do inside the Ardas

lines: MOST OF THE ARDAS IS INHERITED.
ONE PART NO ONE CAN WRITE FOR YOU.
cards: Most of the Ardas is inherited. The words about the ten Gurus, the martyrs, vichhora, rising spirits and good for all come down through generations, the same in a village in Punjab and a suburb in California.

But there's one part no one can write for you: the petition, the reason today. It can be said in Punjabi, in English, in a whisper, in the words of a seven-year-old asking for her cat to get better. And it's still Ardas.

teach.h: WE BEG, AND THE GIVER GIVES.
teach.b: Sikh teaching doesn't treat personal asking as something embarrassing. Guru Nanak says it plainly in the Japji, in the fourth pauri, on ang 2: we speak, we beg, give, give, and the Giver gives. The asking is expected.
What Sikhs often add is a sense of how to ask.

A petition is called a benti, a humble request: not a demand, not a bargain, not a list of grievances. Think back over this week. Fateh: the victory belongs to God, so no one has to pretend to control the outcome.
Karah prashad: begin with thanks. Before a journey: name the task honestly. In grief: ask for the strength to accept the Will, not only for the pain to stop.
In joy: thanks, with nothing added. Standing: come ready to act on what you ask. Put those together and you have something like a shape for a personal petition, without anyone handing you the words.
First, what you're thankful for. Then what you're asking, plainly. Then who else it's for, because the Ardas always widens.
Some Sikhs also add a line of acceptance, that whatever comes is within the Will. The words themselves are yours, and nobody grades them.
An Ardas said in clumsy English by a teenager at 2 a.m. is still Ardas.
An honest, clumsy benti fits that word better than a beautiful one that isn't meant.

how: Sikhs place their own request into the Ardas at the petition, in Punjabi or any language; at home a person praying alone names their reason in their own words.

o: a fixed prayer text everyone recites
a vow promising a gift in return
a humble request, said in your own words

games.q: your own petition — tap the pairs.
p: we beg, and the Giver gives

s: the petition in the Ardas must be said in Punjabi
it can be said in any language, even a whisper.
Guru Nanak treats asking the Giver as expected
Japji, pauri 4: we speak, we beg, and the Giver gives.
a personal petition needs beautiful words to count
honest and clumsy is still Ardas.

games.q: it's 2 a.m. you want to pray but don't know the proper words. what does Sikh practice say?
o: wait until you learn the right words.
say it honestly, in your own words.
games.why: the petition is yours. a benti in clumsy English at 2 a.m. is still Ardas.

practice: Compose three lines, in your head or in your phone's notes: something you're thankful for today, the one thing you most want to ask for, and someone else this is for. Don't polish them or make them sound holy; just make them true.
If you pray, you can offer them inside your own prayer or after a quiet Waheguru; if not, simply read them back to yourself.

wordCard.voice: Benti, a humble request: inside the inherited Ardas, the reason for today is said in your own words, in any language.

orig.note: Gurmukhi: a humble request or supplication; in Gurbani often spelled ਬੇਨੰਤੀ.

carryVoice: Your line: your own words. Clumsy and honest is enough for a benti. See you next time.
